MPs have warned that delays in regulating high-risk Brazilian butt lifts could leave patients exposed to serious safety risks, including infections and complications.


## MPs Raise Fresh Concerns Over Delayed Brazilian Butt Lift Ban


Members of Parliament have renewed calls for tighter restrictions on high-risk cosmetic procedures, warning that delays in government action could continue to expose patients to serious health and safety risks.


The warning comes from the UK Parliament's Women and Equalities Committee, which has previously called for an immediate ban on certain high-risk procedures, including liquid Brazilian Butt Lifts, commonly known as liquid BBLs.


The committee says it remains concerned that invasive cosmetic treatments are still being performed by people who may not have the specialist training required to carry them out safely.


According to evidence previously presented to MPs, some procedures involving scalpels and significant amounts of anaesthetic have allegedly been performed in private homes and commercial beauty salons rather than appropriate clinical environments.


The committee has now expressed disappointment that it has not received a government response to its recommendations nearly seven months after its original report.


## What Is a Brazilian Butt Lift?


A Brazilian Butt Lift is a cosmetic procedure designed to alter the shape and appearance of the buttocks. Traditional BBL surgery generally involves transferring fat from another part of the body to the buttocks.


A liquid BBL is different. Instead of using a patient's own fat, practitioners may inject a substance or filler to increase volume and change the shape of the buttocks.


Because injectable cosmetic procedures can carry significant medical risks, concerns have grown about treatments being offered outside properly regulated medical settings.


The latest parliamentary warning specifically highlights liquid BBLs as an area where stronger restrictions may be necessary.


## Why Are MPs Concerned About Patient Safety?


The Women and Equalities Committee has described some high-risk cosmetic procedures as presenting a serious threat to patient safety.


Christine Jardine, interim chairwoman of the committee, said MPs had previously recommended immediate action on procedures considered particularly dangerous, including liquid BBLs and liquid breast augmentation.


The committee argues that continuing delays mean patients could remain exposed to procedures that are being delivered without sufficient safeguards.


One of the major concerns is the involvement of practitioners who may not possess appropriate specialist qualifications or training.


Cosmetic treatments can sometimes be marketed as relatively straightforward procedures, but invasive interventions can involve substantial medical risks. Where procedures involve injections, incisions, anaesthetic or other invasive techniques, complications may require urgent medical attention.


For this reason, MPs are calling for stronger professional requirements for practitioners carrying out invasive cosmetic surgery.


## Reports Highlight Complications Following Liquid BBL Procedures


Evidence presented to the committee has also highlighted the experiences of patients who have suffered complications following cosmetic procedures.


Ashton Collins, co-founder of Save Face, a register for medical aesthetic practitioners, told MPs that the situation had become increasingly concerning.


According to the information cited by the committee, Save Face has assisted more than 1,200 women who experienced complications following liquid BBLs or liquid breast augmentation.


The evidence presented to MPs indicated that more than half of these patients developed sepsis and required hospital treatment.


A further 40% reportedly required extensive corrective surgery or continuing care from district nursing services.


These figures illustrate why health professionals and policymakers are calling for greater oversight of high-risk cosmetic procedures.


However, individual patient outcomes can vary considerably, and complications can depend on the treatment performed, the substances used, the practitioner's qualifications, the clinical environment and the patient's individual circumstances.


## Concerns Over Procedures Being Performed in Unsafe Settings


Another major issue raised by MPs is where invasive cosmetic procedures are being carried out.


The committee previously heard allegations that procedures involving scalpels and large quantities of anaesthetic were taking place in residential properties and salons.


A properly equipped medical environment is important when a procedure carries a risk of serious complications. Appropriate clinical facilities can provide access to trained staff, sterile equipment, emergency support and systems for managing complications.


The concerns raised by MPs therefore extend beyond the procedure itself. They also involve the qualifications of the person carrying out the treatment and the environment in which it takes place.


For people considering cosmetic surgery or injectable treatments, these factors are important considerations when assessing the safety of a provider.


## MPs Call for Specialist Training and Certification


The Women and Equalities Committee is calling for practitioners who perform invasive surgical cosmetic procedures to have specialist training and appropriate board certification for the procedures they undertake.


MPs also want the government to establish a clear timetable for broader reform of the cosmetic surgery and aesthetics sector.


The committee has argued that professional standards should be strengthened, particularly for procedures that present a higher risk of serious harm.


It also welcomed plans for a licensing system covering non-surgical cosmetic procedures, but said that progress in regulating the sector needs to happen more quickly.


The broader debate reflects growing concerns about how cosmetic treatments are marketed and delivered in the UK.


## What Should Patients Consider Before a Cosmetic Procedure?


While regulatory reform remains a matter for policymakers, people considering cosmetic procedures can take steps to reduce avoidable risks.


Patients should research the practitioner carefully and ask about their qualifications, specialist training and experience with the specific procedure.


It is also important to understand exactly what substance, product or technique will be used. Patients should be given clear information about potential risks, expected results, alternatives and what will happen if complications occur.


The setting should also be considered. People should be cautious about invasive treatments being offered in environments that do not appear suitable for medical procedures.


Patients may also want to ask whether there is appropriate aftercare and what emergency arrangements are available if something goes wrong.


Importantly, anyone experiencing worrying symptoms following a cosmetic procedure should seek appropriate medical advice rather than relying solely on online information or advice from an aesthetic practitioner.


## The Wider Debate About Cosmetic Surgery Regulation


The controversy surrounding liquid BBLs forms part of a wider discussion about cosmetic surgery regulation in the UK.


The cosmetic aesthetics market has expanded considerably, offering consumers an increasing number of treatments designed to change or enhance appearance.


While many procedures may be carried out safely by appropriately trained professionals, MPs and industry bodies have raised concerns about treatments being offered by inadequately trained practitioners.


The committee's latest warning puts renewed pressure on the government to respond to recommendations concerning high-risk procedures.


For patients, the central issue is straightforward: cosmetic treatment should not come at the expense of basic medical safety standards.


## What Happens Next?


The Women and Equalities Committee is urging the government to act on its previous recommendations and introduce restrictions on the highest-risk cosmetic procedures.


MPs also want clearer requirements for practitioners performing invasive procedures and a timetable for wider reform of the sector.


Until further measures are introduced, the committee says patients could remain exposed to unnecessary risks.


The debate over a potential Brazilian Butt Lift ban is therefore not simply about cosmetic preferences. It is increasingly focused on professional standards, clinical environments, informed consent and the protection of people seeking aesthetic treatments.


For anyone considering a BBL or another invasive cosmetic procedure, researching the practitioner, understanding the risks and choosing an appropriate clinical setting remain important steps before treatment.


**Source:** The Independent, 11 September 2026.


### Disclaimer


This article is provided for general informational purposes and does not constitute medical advice. It is not intended to diagnose, treat or prevent any medical condition. Cosmetic procedures can carry serious risks, and individual circumstances vary. Anyone considering a Brazilian Butt Lift, liquid BBL or other cosmetic procedure should seek advice from an appropriately qualified medical professional and independently verify the practitioner's qualifications, registration, facilities and aftercare arrangements.
